The poem is a double sestina whose form is defined by a fixed rotation of six end-words (mountains/valleys/forests/music/morning/evening) across its twelve six-line stanzas and three-line envoi. The rotation realized by the supplied text is exactly the canonical pattern, so the two misplaced lines must be a pair that share the same end-word; only then can the rotation remain intact while the poem is nevertheless disordered.

Inspection of every line that terminates on “music” isolates precisely two candidates whose content is incongruous with its present location:

- Line 25 (“These forests eke, made wretched by our music”) produces a subject–verb disagreement with the following line (“Hath made itself…”).  
- Line 74 (“Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music”) is a clause fragment that belongs at the head of a stanza, not in the envoi.

Exchanging these two lines restores grammatical continuity (“…music / Hath made itself…”) and yields the expected envoi (“These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys, / These forests eke, made wretched by our music”). No other pair satisfies both the formal constraint and the textual evidence.

Thus the swapped lines are 25 and 74.
